name: Preparedness paradox
statement: Preparation that works leaves no disaster to point at, so the money it cost is judged afterwards as an overreaction.
meaning: Two separable claims sit inside the name. The first is about perception: harm that was prevented leaves nothing for anyone to weigh against the cost, so the cost stands alone and looks excessive. The second is about incentives: officials who expect that reading spend on visible response rather than on invisible prevention. The first is a claim about how people judge counterfactuals, and no test of it was located. The second is a claim about political behaviour, and one quantitative study supports a weaker version of it. The name also carries at least three other ideas in print. In business and disaster research a preparedness paradox is usually the gap between how worried people say they are and how little they do about it. In epidemiology the near-identical prevention paradox belongs to Geoffrey Rose and means something else again. In pandemic research a paradox usually names low uptake of a precaution during an outbreak, as in the 2009 H1N1 vaccination rates studied by Reintjes and colleagues across five European countries.

origin.who: Chris Hayes, quoting a doctor he did not name
origin.note: The claim in its present form spread in March 2020 under the name 'paradox of preparation'. Jason Kottke quoted Hayes on 16 March 2020: the only way to get ahead of the curve is to take actions that at the time seem like overreactions. Who first put 'preparedness paradox' in print could not be established. Wikipedia dates the phrase to a 1949 United States Senate armed services subcommittee hearing quoting General Bradley, citing a Google Books snippet that could not be opened for this entry. The earliest peer-reviewed title carrying the phrase that a Crossref title search returns is Kruger, Fernandes, Cupal and Homish in 2019, whose abstract could not be obtained either.

evidence: No study of the claim itself was located. The nearest quantitative evidence is about voters. Healy and Malhotra used data on natural disasters, government spending and election returns in the United States, and report that voters reward the incumbent presidential party for delivering disaster relief spending but not for investing in preparedness. They estimate that $1 spent on preparedness is worth about $15 in future damage mitigated. Their full text is paywalled and could not be obtained here, so this comes from the abstract at the publisher and no coefficients are quoted. What they measure is how voters treat money already spent, not how anyone judges a disaster that did not happen. Weller and Jamieson ran two online survey experiments with over 3,400 respondents in the setting of covid-19, and found that information about how well preparedness works raised support for it, including among people whose prior belief was that public health programmes were ineffective. That is also read from the abstract, deposited with Crossref by the publisher. Gissing, Van Leeuwen, Tofa and Haynes surveyed the central business district of Lismore in New South Wales, where a levee built in 2005 for A$21 million protects against floods up to a one-in-ten-year event. Fifty of about 400 flood-prone businesses answered by telephone in November 2016 and February 2017. Thirty-two per cent expected to flood less often than once a decade, which overstates what the levee was built to do. Thirty-four per cent said preparing mattered less than it had before the levee. Eighty per cent had a flood action plan, against 97% of the 73 businesses surveyed in 2002. The levee overtopped in March 2017, and of 15 businesses asked afterwards, 14 said the community had grown less prepared since it went up.

replication.headline: No test of the claim was located, and no original study of it exists to repeat.
replication.detail: The proposition is that averted harm gets judged as harm that was never coming. A search for any study measuring that judgement returned nothing. Europe PMC full-text search for the phrase returns three papers, none of them about it. A Crossref title search returns seven, on life history theory, climate attitudes, business continuity, Zambian tourism, flood readiness in the United Arab Emirates, cold weather in Ukraine and ageing in Peru. The one whose abstract was obtainable, Day and Dennis on business disruption, uses the name for leaders who fail to act on warnings, which is the opposite failure to the one this entry describes.

limits: The two cases the claim is usually argued from do not carry it. Y2K is the first. Quiggin puts world spending at as much as US$500 billion and Australian spending at A$12 billion, and reports that no serious evaluation after the event was made. His argument runs the other way. Problems were slight even where little remediation was done, Italy's official body first met in February 1999 and confined its work to critical systems, and eastern European countries largely ignored the problem without seeing the failures the standard account predicted. He also names the trap: the absence of any serious Y2K problems could always be attributed to the success of the remediation programme, so the claim cannot lose. He adds that incentives ran towards spending rather than away from it, because nobody was blamed for overspending while the risk of litigation for underspending was real. The version read here is the February 2004 University of Queensland working paper; the published version appeared in the Australian Journal of Public Administration in 2005. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic is the second. The review committee convened under the International Health Regulations, chaired by Harvey Fineberg, reported to the World Health Assembly on 5 May 2011 and dealt with the charge that WHO had overstated the danger. Its answer was that reasonable criticism can be based only on what was known at the time and not on what was later learnt. Of 899 patients admitted in Mexico between late March and 1 June 2009, 58 became critically ill, and 41% of those died. In August 2009 the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology in the United States sketched a scenario of 30,000 to 90,000 American deaths, and the midpoint and upper end proved to be five times the post-pandemic estimate of the actual number. Even so, 87% of deaths were in people under 65. That is a forecast corrected by events rather than a disaster held off by preparation, and the committee nowhere credits the response with the mild outcome. It found no evidence of commercial influence on WHO decisions, and it found real faults, among them the absence of any consistent measure of severity. Its lead conclusion was that the world is ill-prepared to respond to a severe influenza pandemic. Attempts to open the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly's pages on its own 2010 inquiry returned an error, so nothing is claimed here about what that body resolved. Searching covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic text, Europe PMC full text, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, Google Books and general web search. OpenAlex and HathiTrust were not reachable. Three documents wanted for this entry could not be opened: the full text of Healy and Malhotra, the abstract of Kruger and colleagues, and the 1949 hearing.
misreadings: Rose's prevention paradox is a different idea, and merging the two is the commonest error. His 1981 paper in the BMJ puts it as a measure that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual. His examples are arithmetic rather than psychology. Mass diphtheria immunisation in Britain 40 years earlier took roughly 600 children immunised for one life saved. If all male British doctors wore seat belts on every journey of their working lives, about 400 would take the precaution for each life saved, and 399 would buckle up every day for 40 years without benefit to their survival. From the Framingham data, a man of average coronary risk who cut his serum cholesterol by 0.65 mmol/l for life had about a one in 50 chance of avoiding coronary heart disease before 55, one in 25 in a group with mild hypertension and smoking, and one in 400 and one in 150 for women in those two groups. Rose's conclusion is that individual health education will not motivate people, because there is little in it for each of them. Nothing in it concerns how averted harm is judged afterwards. The wording usually quoted, which inserts 'preventative' before 'measure', comes from the 2008 book Rose's Strategy of Preventive Medicine rather than from the 1981 paper, as Thompson's citation shows. The Lismore result belongs to a third idea again, called the levee effect or the safe development paradox, in which protective works lower readiness for the flood that eventually arrives. Healy and Malhotra get cited as proof that preparation is punished. What they report is that relief is rewarded and preparedness is not, which is indifference rather than punishment, and their outcome is votes rather than any judgement about a counterfactual. Naming the pattern settles nothing about whether a given preparation was worth its price. Whether harm was averted is the point in dispute, and the paradox as usually stated assumes the answer.
